newsitem.title: CANADA: Economists relieved at Canada unemployment drop.
newsitem.headline: Economists relieved at Canada unemployment drop.

text.p: Canada's unemployment rate, which spiked into double digits in June, returned in August to the more usual level of 9.4 percent, Statistics Canada said on Friday.
Prime Minister Jean Chretien had characterized the rise in June to 10.0 percent as a mere "blip" but when it fell to only 9.8 percent in July, some eyebrows began to be raised.
"I finally exhaled after two months of wondering where the jobs were," Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC) senior economist John Clinkard said.
Chretien has relied for job creation mainly on lower interest rates stemming from steadily falling budget deficits.

"We're thrilled. The government is trying hard to put the fundamentals of the economy on track and the unemployment rate just proves that what we're doing is right," Chretien spokeswoman Leslie Swartman told Reuters.
The 82,000 jobs created in August, to a total of 13.72 million, was the highest in more than three years and more than offset job losses in June. For the year to date, 153,000 jobs have been created.
The unemployment rate has fallen from a peak of 11.9 percent in late 1992, but Chretien has been unable to push it below nine percent.
Since October 1994 it has been stuck between nine and 10 percent, almost double the 5.1 percent announced on Friday in the neighboring United States, where job creation was also strong.

In the near term, the better numbers here and in the United States made it more unlikely that the Bank of Canada, which had been aggressively lowering interest rates independent of U.S. rates, would lower Canadian rates further.
"Those prospects at this juncture have all but vanished," said senior economist David Rosenberg at brokerage Nesbitt Burns.
"If you are lowering rates in advance of a potential U.S. increase, you put yourself at some risk," CIBC's Clinkard said.
The Canadian dollar opened a bit firmer at C$1.3712 from Thursday's close of C$1.3730.

Rosenberg highlighted the 51,000 new jobs in Ontario, the manufacturing heartland of Canada, suggesting that this could help budget revenues exceed expectations and help the bond market rather than harm it.
"My sense is that those revenue projections are being exceeded," echoed Clinkard.

The unemployment rate in Quebec, which is run by a separatist government, fell to 11.8 percent in August from 12.4 percent in July. But job gains only partly offset estimated losses from June and July.
